newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian koala dilemma - to cuddle or to eat?.
newsitem.headline: Australian koala dilemma - to cuddle or to eat?.

text.p: Australian conservationists said on Monday koalas were worth over a billion tourist dollars last year, while a leading academic suggested the cuddly icon could become a useful source of food.
The Australian Koala Foundation (AKF) released a study which it said showed A$1.1 billion was injected into the economy in 1996 by tourists interested in seeing the uniquely Australian marsupials.
The study said koalas were also directly or indirectly responsible for 9,000 jobs in tourism and wildlife care.

But while conservationists argued that the economic worth of koalas made their conservation imperative, an academic asked why the dozy, teddy bear-like animals were not a regular part of the Australian diet.
"Why can't I sit down to a koala steak or a breast of sulphur-crested cockatoo?" professor Joe Baker said in the keynote address to a waste resources conference in Brisbane.
Australia had developed European-style food chains in the 209 years since white settlement despite vast climate differences between the two continents, Baker told Compost '97.
Baker, head of the Canberra-based Commission for the Environment, said responsible resource management should mean that a wide range of native Australian animals could be harvested for food.
"...I can eat mudcrabs, prawns, bream or whiting without a murmur of protest because seafood was widely accepted as a sustainable food resource," Baker said.
Yet protests from "extremist greenies in the United States" saw resistance to the use of kangaroos, another Australian marsupial, as food, he said.
The AKF study was based on a survey of 419 departing foreign tourists, 22 percent of whom said the unique wildlife was a factor in their decision to visit Australia.
Asked which animals they wanted to see most, 72 percent of respondents nominated koalas.
The survey sample, conducted at Sydney and Brisbane airports, included 115 Japanese visitors.
The AKF argued that the survey, undertaken by the Australia Institute and the University of Queensland, showed that koalas were one of Australia's most important economic resources.
"If Australia ensures the survival of the koala, it will provide an income that is secure into the future," AKF executive director Deborah Tabart said in a statement.
The AKF survey was launched by John Brown, a former Australian tourism minister who once described the koala as "flea-ridden, it piddles on you, it stinks and it scratches".
Koalas numbers are estimated at between 40,000 and 80,000.
